title: Object-Oriented Programming
description: Modeling with modern Java, the SOLID principles in practice and the most used design patterns.
resumo: Sealed types list exactly who may implement them; a switch over them is exhaustive without `default`.
Pattern matching tests a type and binds a variable in one step; specific cases before general ones.
High cohesion, low coupling: depend on interfaces, receive dependencies in the constructor.
SRP: one reason to change (not one method). OCP: extend with new implementations, not edits.
LSP: no `UnsupportedOperationException` for your own contract — split it (ISP). DIP: the domain owns the interface.
Strategy in Spring: inject `Map<String, Interface>`; unknown keys fail loudly.
Builder for many optional parameters, validating in `build()`; static factories (`of`, `from`) for simple cases.

subsections.subtitle: Sealed Classes
subsections.description: Closing a hierarchy to a known set of types.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a payment can only be Pix, card or bank slip. With an open interface anyone can add a new type, and code that handles "every type" silently misses it.

**Concept:** a `sealed` class or interface lists in `permits` exactly which types may extend or implement it. Each permitted subtype must be `final`, `sealed` or `non-sealed`. Because the compiler knows the full set, a `switch` over it can be exhaustive without `default`.

**How it works:** combine sealed interfaces with records to model "one of these options" in the domain; the compiler then checks that every option is handled.
examples.interview_question: How do sealed classes help with domain modeling?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Adding `default` to a switch over a sealed type. It throws away the compile-time check: add a new payment type and the switch still compiles, quietly treating it as "other".

subsections.subtitle: Pattern Matching
subsections.description: Testing a type and using it in one step.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** checking a type and then casting — `if (obj instanceof String) { String s = (String) obj; }` — repeats the type and makes it easy to cast to the wrong one.

**Concept:** pattern matching for `instanceof` (Java 16) tests the type and declares a variable in one step. Pattern matching for `switch` (Java 21) chooses by type, with guards (`when`) and record patterns that unpack a record's components.

**How it works:** use it at the edges of the system, where values of different types arrive. When the behavior belongs to the type itself, a method on the type (polymorphism) is still better than a switch.
examples.interview_question: How does pattern matching make type checks safer and more readable?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Putting a general case before a more specific one. The specific case could never run, so the compiler rejects the switch. Specific (guarded) cases go first.

subsections.subtitle: Cohesion and Coupling
subsections.description: Two measures of a design that is easy to change.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a change in the report format breaks email sending; testing one class needs a real database. Both are signs of a design that is hard to change.

**Concept:** cohesion is how related a class's responsibilities are: a highly cohesive class does one thing well. Coupling is how much a class depends on the details of others: with low coupling you can replace one part without a cascade of changes. The goal is high cohesion and low coupling.

**How it works:** depend on interfaces, receive dependencies through the constructor, and avoid catch-all "Utils" or "Manager" classes.
examples.interview_question: What does "high cohesion and low coupling" mean?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A "Manager" class that does everything — saving, emailing, generating PDFs, calculating tax. It has many reasons to change, and every change risks the others. Split it so each class has one reason to change.

subsections.subtitle: Introduction to SOLID
subsections.description: Five guidelines for classes that are easy to change.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** code that works today, but where every change breaks something else. SOLID are five guidelines to keep classes easy to change.

**Concept:** S — Single Responsibility: a class has one reason to change. O — Open/Closed: extend behavior by adding code, not by editing code that works. L — Liskov Substitution: a subtype must work wherever its base type is expected. I — Interface Segregation: small, focused interfaces. D — Dependency Inversion: high-level code depends on abstractions, not on implementations; Spring's dependency injection applies it.

**How it works:** use them as questions during design and code review, not as rules to apply everywhere — over-applying them adds abstractions nobody needs.
examples.interview_question: Briefly explain each letter of SOLID.

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Breaking Liskov. The classic case is `Square extends Rectangle`: keeping the sides equal breaks code written for `Rectangle`. If a subtype cannot keep the base type's promises, it should not extend it.

subsections.subtitle: SRP and OCP in Practice
subsections.description: One reason to change; extend without editing.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** `OrderService` calculates the total, saves to the database, generates the invoice PDF and sends the email. It has 600 lines and four reasons to change, and each change risks the other three.

**Concept:** the Single Responsibility Principle says a class should have one reason to change — one group of people asking for changes to it. The Open/Closed Principle says new behavior should come in as new code (a new implementation) instead of edits to code that is already tested.

**How it works:** extract each responsibility into a collaborator and let the service orchestrate. A new notification channel is then a new `Notifier` implementation; `OrderService` does not change.
examples.interview_question: Give an example of an SRP violation and how you would fix it.

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Reading SRP as "one method per class". The code splinters into dozens of tiny classes that only make sense together, and following one feature means opening ten files. The unit of SRP is a reason to change, not a method.

subsections.subtitle: LSP, ISP and DIP
subsections.description: Safe substitution, lean interfaces and inverted dependencies.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** subclasses that throw "not supported", interfaces with twelve methods that most implementations leave empty, and services that create their own database client.

**Concept:** Liskov Substitution: a subtype must work wherever its base type is expected, with no surprises — no stricter inputs, no weaker guarantees, no `UnsupportedOperationException`. Interface Segregation: small interfaces shaped for each client, so nobody implements methods they do not need. Dependency Inversion: high-level policy owns the abstraction, and low-level details implement it.

**How it works:** with DIP, the domain declares `PaymentGateway`; the infrastructure provides `PixGateway`. The checkout depends only on the interface, so it can be tested with a fake and the provider can change.
examples.interview_question: Explain the Liskov Substitution Principle with an example of a violation.

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: An implementation that throws for a method of its contract. Code written for the interface breaks with this one type. Split the contract (ISP), so each type only promises what it can do.

subsections.subtitle: Strategy with Spring
subsections.description: Interchangeable algorithms, chosen at runtime without a switch.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** discount campaigns are chosen with a `switch` on the campaign code. Every month a new campaign edits the same `switch`.

**Concept:** the Strategy pattern puts each algorithm in its own class behind a common interface, and the caller picks one at runtime. In Spring, every implementation can be injected at once as a `Map<String, Interface>`, keyed by bean name — the `switch` disappears.

**How it works:** a new campaign is a new `@Component` with its name; `PriceService` does not change.
examples.interview_question: When should you use Strategy instead of an if/else chain?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A silent fallback for an unknown key. A typo in the campaign code ("BLACKFRIDAY") quietly means "no discount", and nobody notices until customers complain. Unknown keys should fail loudly.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** `new Order(null, null, true, 3)` — what does `true` mean? And which shipping client should be created for this carrier?

**Concept:** a Factory hides which concrete class is created — for example, choosing the shipping client by carrier — so callers depend only on the interface. A Builder creates objects with many optional parameters step by step, avoiding "telescoping" constructors and unreadable calls. For simple objects, prefer records and static factory methods (`of`, `from`).

**How it works:** Lombok's `@Builder`, or a static nested `Builder` class, provides the fluent API; `build()` is where the object is validated.
examples.interview_question: When should you use a Builder instead of a constructor?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A builder whose `build()` accepts anything. The constructor's validation is gone, and invalid objects appear again. Check the required fields in `build()`.
